cells.tense: You are already pointed somewhere, and your hands are steady on the wheel.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're pulled toward and put a date on it this week — something you'd actually do that day. Tell one person the date before it passes.
cells.core:
Nothing about this is loud. You're walking toward something you can't fully see, and the walking is its own kind of good. When a pull is real it lands without argument — that's how you can tell which one is yours, and not just whichever voice is loudest in the room.

Here is what it looks like on a good day: you choose, you say so, you move, and the room around you settles because someone is pointing. Where your direction is steady, other people move more freely than they otherwise would. That's worth feeding. And this is a good week to pick, because the ground before any decision is still soft enough to hold a new weight. So put a date on the thing you're pulled toward, and let one person know the date.
cells.sheetLine: You're pointed somewhere real. Put a date on it.

cells.place: the room before any door has been painted

cells.tense: You are deciding a direction for a life that hasn't shown up yet.
cells.ask: Bring one decision down to today — the smallest real version of it, done before bed. Set the other directions aside. Choose the one with the soonest consequence.
cells.core:
The future version of your life is more real to you than the floor you're standing on, and you keep picking for it. Nothing you choose feels finished, because the room it's for keeps receding.

Underneath the bracing there's something you can use: an eye sharp enough to hold several true things at once, and a preference that already knows what it wants. That knowing doesn't need defending or proof. Point it at one small thing with an end on it, a decision you can complete today. The rest can wait. The person you're deciding for isn't here yet — but someone is.

cells.tense: You are standing still with a choice behind you, saying it isn't made.
cells.ask: Say what you're pulled toward to one person this week — a friend, a call, a voicemail if that's what it takes. Say it plain, without arguing for it.
cells.core:
Asked what you want, your voice goes careful, like the answer might be more than it's worth to say. The quiet is real, and it sits after a step rather than in front of one.

Something still pulls you toward a direction. You can watch it steer what you notice and where your attention goes. There's no forcing that back out — only saying it. Try it with one person who can hear it without trying to fix it. If it lands badly, that's information, not a verdict. Say it once, in your own voice, and let it stand where it lands.
cells.sheetLine: Something still pulls you. You've just stopped saying it.

cells.tense: You are already pointing somewhere and keep calling the direction open.
cells.ask: For one week, when you start to say you're not sure about something, notice if something in you has already leaned. Say the lean, once. Then carry on with the day.
cells.core:
A direction is running under your days — it decides which conversations you stay in, what you pick up to read, who you make room for. And it gets described as though it hadn't happened yet. The steering is quiet. It's also accurate.

Notice the moment uncertainty comes out of your mouth and something in you has already moved. That moving is your own choosing, doing its work where anyone could see it. No plan is needed, and no permission is needed to follow it. You're already following it. All that's left is the small admission that you're the one pointing. Which pull to follow can stay open as long as it likes.
cells.sheetLine: You're already pointed somewhere. Say the lean out loud once.
